events/zara-yaqob-reforms-1450/title: Zara Yaqob's council and Ethiopian church reforms
events/zara-yaqob-reforms-1450/summary: Emperor Zara Yaqob convened a council at Debre Mitmaq (1450) that reconciled the followers of Ewostatewos by accepting observance of both Saturday and Sunday Sabbaths, and promoted Marian devotion and liturgical reform. He also wrote theological treatises and suppressed rival cults harshly.
events/zara-yaqob-reforms-1450/consequen: Distinctive Ethiopian observance of two Sabbaths
events/fall-of-constantinople-1453/summa: On 29 May 1453 the Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople; the last emperor Constantine XI died in battle and Hagia Sophia became a mosque. Mehmed appointed the anti-unionist Gennadios Scholarios patriarch, making him head of the Orthodox millet within the Ottoman Empire.
events/fall-of-constantinople-1453/longT: The fall ended the Roman Empire in the East after more than eleven centuries. Western help had been minimal despite the union of Florence. Under the millet system, the Ecumenical Patriarch became both spiritual and civil head of the Ottoman Orthodox, which preserved the church but also tied it to Ottoman politics, with patriarchs frequently deposed. Greek scholars fleeing west contributed to the Renaissance study of Greek, and thus to Erasmus' Greek New Testament. Moscow, now the most powerful Orthodox state, increasingly claimed Byzantium's mantle. For the Orthodox, the fall began centuries of 'Turkocratia', with neo-martyrs, crypto-Christians and a theology shaped by survival; for the West, it fed crusading proposals and apocalyptic speculation.
events/fall-of-constantinople-1453/conse: Hagia Sophia converted into a mosque
Greek learning in the Renaissance West
events/gutenberg-bible-1455/summary: Johannes Gutenberg's workshop in Mainz completed the first major book printed with movable metal type, a Latin Vulgate Bible. Printing transformed the spread of Scripture, devotional books and, within two generations, Reformation pamphlets.
events/gutenberg-bible-1455/causes/0: Technological innovation and demand for books
events/spanish-inquisition-1478/summary: With papal approval, Ferdinand and Isabella established a royal Inquisition to investigate conversos suspected of secretly practising Judaism. It led to the expulsion of Jews from Spain (1492) and later pursued Moriscos, Protestants and mystics, and operated in Spanish America.
events/malleus-maleficarum-1486/summary: Following Innocent VIII’s bull Summis desiderantes (1484), the Dominican inquisitor Heinrich Kramer published the Malleus Maleficarum at Speyer, presenting witchcraft as a real, largely female conspiracy with the devil to be punished by torture and death.
events/malleus-maleficarum-1486/causes/0: Late medieval fusion of demonology, heresy trials and magic
events/malleus-maleficarum-1486/conseque: Became a reference work in some witch trials, though many courts and inquisitors (notably the Spanish and Roman Inquisitions) treated it with caution
Its misogynist theory has made it a symbol of the witch-hunts
events/conversion-of-kongo-1491/title: Conversion of the Kingdom of Kongo
events/conversion-of-kongo-1491/summary: Portuguese priests baptised the Manikongo Nzinga a Nkuwu (João I) at Mbanza Kongo in May 1491. His son Afonso I (r. 1509–1543) made Catholicism the religion of the kingdom, building an African Christian state with its own literate elite that lasted for centuries.
events/conversion-of-kongo-1491/causes/0: Portuguese voyages down the African coast
events/conversion-of-kongo-1491/conseque: Entanglement with the Portuguese slave trade
events/spanish-conquest-of-americas-1492: Columbus and the beginning of Spanish conquest in the Americas

Columbus' landfall in the Caribbean in October 1492 began the Spanish conquest of the Americas. Papal bulls (1493) granted Spain rights over new lands in return for evangelisation, and the patronato real gave the crown control of the church. Conquest, forced labour and epidemic disease devastated Indigenous peoples, even as friars preached and some protested.

The Iberian conquest joined evangelisation to empire. The encomienda system placed Indigenous people under Spanish lords obliged to Christianise them, and the requerimiento read to them demanded submission to pope and crown. Within a century, epidemic disease and violence reduced Indigenous populations catastrophically. Dominicans such as Antonio de Montesinos (1511) and Bartolomé de las Casas denounced the abuses, leading to the New Laws (1542) and the Valladolid debate (1550–51) on the humanity and rights of Indigenous peoples. Franciscans, Dominicans, Augustinians and later Jesuits baptised millions, built churches and learned languages, while Indigenous Christianity developed its own forms, such as devotion to Our Lady of Guadalupe. Latin American Christians today interpret this legacy variously: as the birth of a mestizo Catholic culture, as an evangelisation compromised by conquest, or as an injustice requiring repentance, as Popes John Paul II and Francis acknowledged in apologies.

Debates over just war and human rights
events/savonarola-executed-1498/summary: The Dominican friar Girolamo Savonarola preached apocalyptic repentance, dominated Florentine politics after 1494 and staged 'bonfires of the vanities'. Excommunicated by Alexander VI, he was hanged and burned on 23 May 1498.
events/savonarola-executed-1498/conseque: Admired by later reformers Catholic and Protestant
events/afonso-of-kongo-1506/title: Afonso I builds a Christian Kongo
events/afonso-of-kongo-1506/summary: Afonso I Mvemba a Nzinga won the throne in 1506 and promoted Catholicism, schools and literacy; his son Henrique was consecrated titular bishop in 1518, the first sub-Saharan African bishop of the Latin church. Afonso's letters to the king of Portugal protest the ravages of the slave trade.
events/afonso-of-kongo-1506/consequences: Kongolese Catholic culture lasting into the 18th century
Early African critique of the slave trade
events/portuguese-goa-1510/summary: Afonso de Albuquerque seized Goa, which became the capital of Portugal's Asian empire and seat of a bishopric (1534) and archbishopric (1558). Under the padroado the crown controlled missions across Asia; the Goa Inquisition (1560) pursued converts accused of Hindu practices.
events/portuguese-goa-1510/consequences/: Base for Xavier and Asian missions
Pressure on Thomas Christians toward Latin rites
events/ninety-five-theses-1517/summary: On 31 October 1517 the Augustinian friar and professor Martin Luther sent his Ninety-five Theses against the sale of indulgences to Archbishop Albrecht of Mainz, and by tradition posted them on the Wittenberg Castle Church door. Printed and spread rapidly, they began the controversy that became the Protestant Reformation.
events/ninety-five-theses-1517/longText: Luther's protest targeted the indulgence campaign of Johann Tetzel, which raised money for St Peter's in Rome and to pay Albrecht's debts. The theses questioned whether the pope had power over purgatory and insisted that true repentance is lifelong, not purchased. Luther's deeper conviction, developed in lectures on Psalms and Romans, was that righteousness before God is a gift received by faith in Christ, not achieved by works. Within three years the debate had moved from indulgences to papal authority, councils and the sacraments; in 1520 Luther published his great Reformation treatises and burned the papal bull Exsurge Domine. The printing press made him Europe's best-selling author. Catholic historians acknowledge the abuses he attacked, many of which Trent reformed, while contending that Luther's doctrine of justification and his rejection of church authority went beyond reform into rupture. Protestants celebrate 31 October as Reformation Day; in 2017 Catholics and Lutherans jointly commemorated the anniversary.
events/christianity-in-philippines-1521/: Magellan's expedition baptised Rajah Humabon and some 800 Cebuanos in April 1521, leaving the image of the Santo Niño. Permanent Spanish evangelisation began with Legazpi in 1565, making the Philippines Asia's largest Catholic nation.
events/diet-of-worms-1521/summary: Summoned before Emperor Charles V, Luther refused to recant unless convinced by Scripture and plain reason, declaring his conscience 'captive to the Word of God'. The Edict of Worms outlawed him, but Frederick the Wise hid him at the Wartburg, where he translated the New Testament into German.
events/zurich-disputation-1523/summary: In January 1523 the Zurich council heard Huldrych Zwingli defend his Sixty-Seven Articles against the bishop of Constance's representatives and authorised him to continue preaching from Scripture, launching the Reformation in Zurich.
events/zurich-disputation-1523/causes/2: Civic control of religion in Swiss cities
events/zurich-disputation-1523/consequen: Abolition of the Mass in Zurich (1525)
Spread to Bern (1528), Basel and other cities
events/franciscan-twelve-mexico-1524/sum: Twelve Franciscans led by Martín de Valencia arrived in New Spain, walked barefoot to Mexico City and were welcomed by Cortés. They and later friars baptised vast numbers, learned Nahuatl and founded schools such as the Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco for Indigenous nobles.
events/first-adult-baptisms-zurich-1525/: On 21 January 1525, after the Zürich council ordered infant baptism, Conrad Grebel baptised George Blaurock in Felix Manz's house, and Blaurock baptised others. The 'rebaptizers' (Anabaptists) sought a free church of committed believers separate from the state; Manz was drowned in 1527.

Grebel and Manz were among Zwingli's most zealous followers, but by 1524 they concluded that the reform was moving too slowly and remained under the city council's control. They found no infant baptism in the New Testament and argued that the church should be a voluntary community of disciples practising mutual discipline. The council's January 1525 disputation decided for infant baptism; that evening the group baptised one another. Persecution was swift — imprisonment, exile and in 1527 the drowning of Manz in the Limmat. The movement spread through Switzerland, South Germany, Austria and the Netherlands, drawing on diverse roots, and was persecuted by Catholics and Protestants alike. Mennonites, Amish, Hutterites and many Baptists honour these first baptisms as the birth of the believers' church tradition; Reformed and Lutheran churches long condemned it but in the 21st century have expressed regret for the persecution.
